A TREATISE ON THE ORDERING OF THE PASSIONS

CHAPTER I

The passions, considered in themselves, are neither good nor evil. It is
in their ordering that virtue consists, and the philosophers of the
ancient schools were agreed upon this much, however they differed after.

CHAPTER II

Resuming the argument: the Stoics held that the passions were errors of
judgement, and that the wise man would be free of them altogether. This
position has been criticised, not without reason, as inhuman.

It has often been observed that the same author will describe the
passions as diseases in one place and as motions of the soul in another.
For example, Seneca does both within a single letter.

CHAPTER III

He said that the remedy lay in habituation, and that no one becomes
temperate by argument alone. According to Aristotle, we become just by
doing just acts.

The reader will see that this book aims to explain rather than to
prescribe, and that its conclusions are offered as observations.
